strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: part-aware reconstruction and kinematic modeling of multi-part articulated objects from multi-view observations.
weaknesses: The main self-supervision claim is overstated: the pipeline relies on large pretrained external models, including a VLM to infer the number of moving components and SAM for mask refinement. These are substantial semantic priors and should not be framed as annotation-free motion discovery alone.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: part-level reconstruction and kinematic modeling of multi-part articulated objects from multi-view observations.

The proposed representation, a latent-conditioned deformable 3D Gaussian field followed by trajectory-based primitive clustering, is a reasonable direction and could be useful if validated more rigorously.

The manuscript attempts to broaden evaluation beyond the very small single-object-per-category settings used in some prior work, and the RS-Art dataset could become a useful resource if released with clear protocols and ground truth.
The paper includes several relevant baselines and reports both geometry and articulation metrics, plus some ablations on refinement and number of interaction states.
weaknesses: The central claims are stronger than the evidence. The method is repeatedly described as fully self-supervised and as not using human priors, but it relies on a pretrained VLM to estimate the number of moving parts and SAM for mask refinement. These are strong external semantic priors, and the paper does not analyze their failure modes, sensitivity, or contribution separately.

The comparison protocol is not convincing. DeGSS receives four interaction states with simultaneous multi-part motion, while several baselines receive only two states or are adapted through per-joint runs and merging. This changes the available motion evidence and makes the headline superiority difficult to interpret as an algorithmic advantage rather than an input/protocol advantage.

The baseline reporting is especially problematic: the paper states that it lists the first run for every method despite observing large run-to-run variance, with no mean/std, confidence intervals, or repeated-trial aggregation. This is not acceptable for a top-tier empirical claim, particularly when some reproduced baselines lack public code.

Important technical details are underspecified: the VLM model and decoding details, number of queried pairs, thresholds, clustering stability, SAM prompting behavior, optimization schedule, Gaussian counts, runtime, and hyperparameter selection are not sufficiently documented for reproducibility.

The joint estimation description appears technically questionable. After Kabsch alignment of two rigid point sets, residuals should be small for both revolute and prismatic rigid motions; the stated rank criterion for distinguishing revolute from prismatic motion is not well justified and seems mathematically suspect. Pivot estimation from static centroids is also unclear and likely fragile.

The evaluation of RS-Art is weak relative to the claims. The main paper presents only qualitative real-data results, and the appendix compares only to ArtGS, stating other baselines could not be made to run reliably. This does not establish broad real-world robustness.

The dataset contribution is promising but not enough as presented: the dataset is small, contains only 18 objects, depends on manually reverse-engineered and manually segmented digital twins, and the release is deferred until publication. This limits both significance and reproducibility at review time.

Ablations are incomplete. The paper does not isolate the effects of the VLM part-count estimator, SAM refinement, boundary splitting, latent deformation field, thresholds, or number of views under a fair shared protocol. The refinement ablation is limited mostly to geometry and a small set of objects.

Novelty is incremental in several components: deformable Gaussian fields, SAM-guided 3D segmentation, trajectory clustering, and articulated-object reconstruction all build heavily on existing ideas. The paper does not clearly separate what is fundamentally new from engineering composition.

Several claims about independent control, collision-free interpolation, automatic part discovery, and stability are based mostly on qualitative examples, without quantitative metrics for interpolation quality, collision rates, part-count accuracy, or robustness to occlusion/camera-pose noise.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: part-aware reconstruction and kinematic modeling of articulated objects from multi-view image observations, with relevance to robotics, AR/VR, and digital twins.

The core idea of representing multiple interaction states as deformations of a shared 3D Gaussian field is technically sensible and well matched to the problem. Using deformation trajectories as cues for unsupervised part segmentation is a clear and useful contribution.
The method addresses a meaningful limitation of prior NeRF/3DGS articulated-object approaches, namely their restriction to two states, a single movable part, or a known part count.

The experimental results are strong across many reported metrics on the expanded PartNet-Mobility split, including joint parameter estimation, part motion, and geometry metrics. The appendix also includes additional three-part object results and ablations.

The proposed RS-Art dataset is a valuable contribution: pairing real RGB-D captures with reverse-engineered articulated digital twins and joint annotations could benefit future work in articulated reconstruction and digital twin modeling.

The paper includes useful ablations on the refinement stage and number of interaction states, and acknowledges important limitations such as occlusion, sparse-state ambiguity, and missing physical properties.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol raises concerns. The paper states that it reports the first run for every method because of baseline variance, rather than averages with standard deviations. This is unusual and weakens confidence in the quantitative comparisons, especially when stability is a major claimed advantage.

The comparison is not fully clean because different methods receive different forms of input and supervision: some baselines are run on single-part sequences, DTArt receives depth and ground-truth part count, and DeGSS receives multiple simultaneous interaction states. The protocol is motivated, but it makes it hard to isolate the benefit of the proposed representation from the acquisition setup.

The claim of being fully self-supervised is somewhat overstated. The method relies on external foundation models, including a VLM to estimate the number of moved components and SAM for mask refinement. These are not manual annotations, but they inject substantial pretrained semantic priors.

Important implementation details are under-specified for reproducibility, including VLM choice and prompting robustness, thresholds, clustering sensitivity, local refinement settings, TSDF extraction parameters, and runtime/training cost.

The real-data evaluation is promising but limited. On RS-Art, the main quantitative comparison appears to be only against ArtGS because other baselines could not be run reliably, which makes the real-world superiority claim less conclusive.

Some methodological components appear heuristic, especially VLM-based part-count estimation, K-means clustering of trajectory descriptors, and recursive Gaussian splitting. The paper would be stronger with sensitivity analyses for these choices and failure cases where the VLM miscounts or motions are coupled/ambiguous.

Novelty is solid but not transformative: the approach combines deformable/dynamic Gaussian splatting, trajectory clustering, SAM-guided segmentation, and articulated fitting. The integration is useful, but several ingredients are adaptations of existing techniques rather than fundamentally new modeling machinery.

The writing contains minor clarity and polish issues, and some claims are stronger than the evidence, especially around automatic part discovery, continuous motion generalization, and applicability to complex real-world settings.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: part-aware reconstruction and kinematic modeling of articulated objects from multi-view images, with relevance to robotics, AR/VR, and digital twins.
The proposed canonical 3D Gaussian field with latent-conditioned state deformation is a reasonable and potentially useful formulation for sharing geometry across interaction states.

The pipeline is ambitious and fairly comprehensive, combining deformation modeling, motion-based part grouping, VLM-based part count estimation, SAM-guided boundary refinement, mesh extraction, joint estimation, interpolation, and real-data evaluation.

The experimental section is broad: it includes expanded PartNet-Mobility results, a new RS-Art real-to-sim dataset, comparisons to several articulated/dynamic reconstruction baselines, ablations, pose-noise tests, runtime reporting, and multi-part cases.
The RS-Art dataset, if released with the promised RGB-D captures, calibrated poses, reverse-engineered meshes, URDF/USD assets, and joint annotations, could be a useful resource for the community.
weaknesses: There are serious technical concerns in the kinematic estimation description. The joint-type identification via Kabsch residual rank appears incorrect: after rigid alignment with rotation and translation, both revolute and prismatic rigid part motions should yield near-zero residuals in the noiseless case, not rank-1 versus full-rank residuals. This undermines confidence in the claimed joint classification and parameter recovery.

The revolute axis/pivot estimation is insufficiently justified. Fitting the pivot axis to static centroids is not a standard consequence of the moving part trajectory and seems unable to robustly identify the true joint location in general. The near-zero axis errors reported therefore need much stronger methodological explanation and validation.

The evaluation protocol is not fully convincing. PD2GS uses four interaction states while key baselines use two-state settings by design, and single-joint baselines are run under different per-part input conditions. The paper gives a two-state PD2GS ablation, but the main headline comparison still mixes different information content across methods.

The paper claims self-supervision, but the method depends heavily on large pretrained external priors: a VLM to infer component counts and SAM for segmentation refinement. This should be positioned more carefully as weakly/external-prior-assisted rather than fully self-supervised.

Several quantitative results are surprisingly strong, often near-perfect on difficult multi-part and real-world settings. Given the technical issues above, limited details on variance, and statements such as reporting the first run rather than averaged runs, the evidence does not yet rule out protocol artifacts or favorable evaluation choices.

The VLM component-count evaluation is very small and likely overfits the chosen categories/prompts. Reporting 100% accuracy on a small set is not enough to establish robustness to ambiguous, occluded, visually subtle, or non-canonical articulations.

The continuous-control claim is only partly supported. Interpolating latent codes and deforming selected Gaussians is visually plausible, but the paper lacks a rigorous evaluation of physical validity, collision avoidance, independent joint control across wider state spaces, or extrapolation beyond observed configurations.

Reproducibility is limited. The manuscript says code and data will be released upon publication, but many implementation details remain underspecified, including deformation network architecture, optimization schedule, hyperparameters, thresholds, VLM model/settings, SAM variant, and sensitivity to these choices.

Real-world evaluation is narrower than the claims suggest. On RS-Art, most baselines reportedly fail or are not run, leaving only ArtGS for quantitative comparison; this weakens the claim of broad real-world superiority.
The manuscript has clarity and polish issues, including formatting/extraction artifacts, inconsistent notation, overstrong claims, and some imprecise descriptions of baseline behavior and fairness.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: self-supervised articulated-object modeling from multi-view, multi-state observations, with relevance to robotics, AR/VR, and digital twins.
The proposed pipeline is practically motivated, combining a shared canonical 3D Gaussian field, latent-conditioned deformations, motion-based part grouping, and SAM-guided boundary refinement.

The manuscript attempts a broad evaluation, including synthetic PartNet-Mobility experiments, higher-part-count cases, unseen-state rendering, ablations, runtime analysis, and a new real-to-sim dataset.
RS-Art could be a useful resource if released with sufficient documentation, calibration details, and evaluation scripts.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is limited. Much of the method appears to be an engineering combination of deformable 3DGS, trajectory clustering, VLM-based part counting, and SAM-based segmentation, without a clearly new modeling principle or strong theoretical insight.

The central self-supervision claim is overstated. The method relies on large pretrained external models, task-specific VLM prompting, SAM masks, hand-tuned thresholds, and a manually reverse-engineered real dataset with part-level articulation annotations for evaluation.

The evaluation protocol is not convincing. PD2GS receives four interaction states while several baselines are inherently two-state methods; equalizing only the total number of images does not equalize the kinematic information available to each method. The two-state ablation is relegated to the appendix and is substantially worse than the main setting.

Baseline handling raises fairness concerns. Single-joint methods are run in a special per-joint mode, multi-joint baselines receive ground-truth part counts, and real-data comparisons largely collapse to ArtGS because other baselines fail. This makes the very large reported gains hard to interpret.

The paper reports the first run rather than averages over multiple seeds, while also mentioning large run-to-run variance. This is not acceptable evidence for a top-tier venue, especially when many tables contain extreme failures or near-perfect results.

Several numerical results look suspicious or insufficiently explained, including near-zero joint errors on complex objects, repeated baseline values across different instances, very large baseline failures dominating means, and inconsistent-looking table formatting. The paper needs stronger auditing of metrics and failure cases.

Important implementation details are missing or vague: the deformation MLP architecture, latent code dimension, optimization schedule, Gaussian initialization, thresholds, VLM identity/settings, SAM variant, clustering settings, local refinement iterations, and mesh extraction parameters are not specified enough for reproducibility.

The continuous-control claim is weakly supported. Interpolating latent codes is shown mostly qualitatively, and there is little evidence that the learned latent space corresponds to physically valid joint coordinates, respects limits, avoids collisions generally, or extrapolates beyond observed poses.

The joint estimation procedure is brittle and under-justified. For example, classifying joint type from residual rank and estimating revolute pivots from static centroids seems heuristic and may fail under noise, partial observation, coupled motion, or non-ideal articulation.

The real-world evaluation is narrow and partly circular: RS-Art is introduced by the authors, has only 18 objects, uses controlled capture and manually reverse-engineered ground truth, and is evaluated against very limited baselines. This is promising but not yet compelling evidence of broad real-world generalization.

Ablations do not isolate the main modeling contribution cleanly. They mostly show that SAM refinement improves segmentation and that more states help, but do not convincingly demonstrate that the proposed deformation formulation is necessary relative to simpler rigid-part or trajectory-fitting alternatives.

Overall, despite an ambitious system and potentially useful dataset, the paper’s claims are stronger than the evidence. The combination of limited novelty, questionable fairness, underspecified implementation, and fragile empirical support makes it not competitive for acceptance at a top-tier AI conference.

strengths: Strong and timely problem formulation: the paper addresses self-supervised articulated object modeling with part-level decoupling, continuous deformation, and kinematic recovery, which is highly relevant for robotics, AR/VR, and digital twins.
The core idea of learning a shared canonical Gaussian field with latent-conditioned state deformations is compelling and well matched to the limitations of prior two-state or single-joint pipelines.

The method is substantially more complete than many prior works: it combines reconstruction, part segmentation, joint type/parameter estimation, and continuous state interpolation within one 3DGS-based framework.

The evaluation is broad and convincing overall, with comparisons against PARIS, ArticulatedGS, DTArt, ArtGS, dynamic NeRF/3DGS baselines, and articulated generation baselines across synthetic and real settings.
The reported gains are large on many important metrics, especially joint axis estimation, part motion, movable-part Chamfer distance, and unseen-state rendering quality.

The proposed RS-Art dataset is a valuable contribution: real RGB-D captures paired with reverse-engineered articulated digital twins and joint annotations would be useful to the community if released as promised.
The appendix is unusually thorough, including multi-part and five-part experiments, robustness to pose perturbations, runtime analysis, two-state variants, and module-level ablations.
weaknesses: The claim of being fully self-supervised is somewhat overstated because the pipeline relies on strong external foundation-model priors, including a VLM for part-count estimation and SAM for boundary refinement, plus calibrated multi-view camera poses.

The evaluation protocol is favorable to the proposed method in some respects: PD2GS uses four interaction states while several baselines are structurally limited to two states, and the equal-image-budget argument does not fully equalize information content.

The paper reports first-run baseline numbers rather than averages with variance, despite acknowledging large run-to-run variance. This weakens confidence in the quantitative margin and makes reproducibility of the comparisons less clear.

Several reported improvements are extremely large, especially on RS-Art and some baseline failures, but the paper provides limited detail on baseline tuning, convergence criteria, and failure handling.

The real-world dataset is promising but still modest in scale, with 18 objects across six categories, and the reverse-engineering process involves manual modeling and annotation effort that may limit scalability.

The method still assumes accurate or reasonably recoverable camera poses, sufficient multi-view coverage, and visible motion cues; performance under severe occlusion, sparse states, textureless/specular surfaces, and unobserved joint limits remains limited.

Continuous control is demonstrated mainly through latent interpolation and qualitative examples; stronger quantitative evaluation of independent joint control, physical validity, and extrapolation beyond observed states would further support the claims.
